proof.text: The valuation domain $V$ and each localization are integrally closed. Indeed, if an integral $a\in K$ did not lie in a given valuation ring, $a^{-1}$ would be a nonunit there; dividing a monic equation for $a$ by its leading power would put $1$ in the maximal ideal. Thus $S$ is normal integral affine. Apply [lem-trf-geometrically-reduced-eta-normal] to the semistable pairs: their curves and markings are reduced and $\eta$-normal. Their generic curves are smooth, since $q_\eta$ is an isomorphism and $Q_\eta$ is smooth. By [lem-trf-valuation-curve-projective-preparation], the normalizations of $P,Q$ are finite $\eta$-modifications. Their $\eta$-normality makes these normalizations isomorphisms, so $P$ and $Q$ are normal. No hypothesis has been added to the item. The horizontal-curve-models lemma [lem-trf-valuation-horizontal-curve-models] also gives finitely many irreducible components of $P$ and $Q$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1(i) and Proposition 3.5.2: derive normality before Lemma 4.4.2

proof.text: The generic fibre is a schematically dense open in every flat $S$-scheme here. If $V$ is not a field, choose $0\ne a$ in its smallest nonzero prime. The finite-chain condition gives $V[1/a]=K$. Flatness implies that multiplication by $a$ is injective on affine coordinate rings, so their localization maps are injective. If $V$ is a field the assertion is immediate. On each normal component of $Q$, schematic density and the generic isomorphism identify its function field with the function field of its inverse-image component in $P$. Reducedness prevents any extra component in the complement of that dense open. Thus [lem-trf-proper-normal-geometric-connectedness], applied componentwise to the proper map $q$, gives nonempty connected geometric fibres. Normal components can be treated separately: the finite-component assertion in Step 1 and normality separate them, and the local-domain condition makes their finite disjoint decomposition open as well as closed.

source.place: Normal-target Zariski connectedness in the proof of Lemma 4.4.2

proof.text: The map $q_M:M\to N$ is an isomorphism. Its fibre over any point of $N$ is contained in a zero-dimensional finite-type marking fibre over a field, hence has finitely many points. By [lem-trf-proper-finite-fibre-finite-near], $q_M$ is finite locally on $N$, therefore finite. It is the given $\eta$-modification, and $N$ is $\eta$-normal by [lem-trf-geometrically-reduced-eta-normal], so it is an isomorphism. This handles the empty marking too. Finiteness of the field-fibre point sets follows from [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] and [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-components]: a zero-dimensional Noetherian scheme has only singleton irreducible components.

source.place: Multipointed marking condition, finite marking modifications and Proposition 3.5.2

proof.text: By [lem-trf-valuation-curve-projective-preparation] the normal modification has a finite modification locus $B\subset Q$, quasi-finite over $S$, and is an isomorphism over $Q\setminus B$. Every $x\in B$ has a positive-dimensional fibre: otherwise its finite-type zero-dimensional fibre is finite, [lem-trf-proper-finite-fibre-finite-near] makes $q$ finite near $x$, and [lem-trf-finite-birational-normal-iso] makes it an isomorphism there, componentwise as in Step 2. Each $x\in B$ is closed in $Q_s$ for its image $s$, because $B_s$ is a finite closed zero-dimensional subscheme. Its fibre $Z=q^{-1}(x)$ is connected by Step 2 and lies in the pure one-dimensional curve $P_s$, Noetherian with finitely many components by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] and [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-components]. A zero-dimensional irreducible component of its support would be a point lying on no one-dimensional component, hence an isolated connected component. Thus $Z$ is pure one-dimensional. It lies entirely in the semistable locus because $(P,M)$ is semistable.

source.place: Locality and quasi-finite modification locus in Lemma 4.4.2; verification of every local-criterion hypothesis

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-valuation-exceptional-local-criterion] at each $x\in B$, to the original family $q$, not to a claimed modification over the residue field. Its hypotheses are now verified: $Q$ is normal, $x$ is closed in its $S$-fibre, $Z$ is a one-dimensional scheme-theoretic fibre in the semistable locus, and $(Q,N)$ is semistable at $x$. It gives an exceptional projective-line tree, including the bound on the boundary plus markings. In particular this establishes reducedness of the actual fibre; none was silently replaced by its reduction. Base change of the scheme-theoretic inverse-image diagram gives the same exceptional trees in $P_\Omega$ for the points of $B_\Omega$. Their complements are the isomorphism locus of $q_\Omega$. This is the local criterion over the original normal total space; normality of the nodal target $Q_\Omega$ is neither asserted nor needed.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.2, both its hypotheses and its forward implication

proof.text: Fix $s$ and $\Omega$, put $r=q_\Omega:(R,L)\to(C,D)$, and let $U=C\setminus B_\Omega$. By [lem-trf-semistable-marked-base-change] both pairs are semistable; [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence] makes $r$ proper. It is surjective with connected geometric fibres by Step 2, and its marking map is an isomorphism by Step 3. The finite set $B_\Omega$ meets no generic point of the pure one-dimensional $C$, so $U$ meets all components and $r^{-1}(U)\simeq U$. The curve $R$ is Noetherian and has finitely many components by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] and [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-components]. Its positive-dimensional fibres are the finitely many disjoint exceptional trees of Step 5. Each such tree has nonempty boundary in $R$: the union of components not contracted by $r$ has closed image containing $U$, hence surjects onto $C$ by properness; it meets that fibre, and connectedness prevents separation from the contracted tree.

source.place: Passage to the geometric pointed curves and Appendix B hypotheses

proof.text: Induct on the total number $e$ of components in these exceptional trees. The induction data are a proper surjective pointed map $r_i:(R_i,L_i)\to(C,D)$ with connected geometric fibres, marking isomorphism, isomorphism over $U$, and reduced supports of positive-dimensional fibres given by disjoint rational trees with nonempty boundary and boundary-plus-marking count at most two. Step 6 supplies $i=0$. If $e>0$, choose such a tree. A one-vertex tree already has at most two special points. If there is more than one vertex, it has at least two leaves. At most two external boundary or marked points are distributed among the vertices, so some leaf carries at most one of them. That leaf component has its one internal node plus at most one external or marked point; hence it meets $L_i\cup(R_i)_{\mathrm{sing}}$ in at most two points. Its image in $C$ is a point and its boundary is nonempty, so the single-component pushout [lem-trf-nodal-exceptional-component-pushout] applies.

source.place: Appendix B before Lemma B.3: explicit leaf selection and finite induction

proof.text: The pushout gives a proper elementary contraction $h_i$ and the remaining pointed map $r_{i+1}$, with all the properness, connectedness, marking and open-isomorphism properties in the induction data. It removes precisely the chosen component. When the tree had other components, its image with the reduced induced structure is the tree with that leaf vertex and adjacent edge deleted. A marked point on the removed leaf moves to the attaching point; an outside boundary on that leaf becomes an outside boundary on the remaining tree. If both had occurred on a nontrivial leaf there would have been three special points, which the choice excludes. Thus no new special point is introduced in the total boundary-plus-marking count. Intersections are the reduced smooth branch points by [lem-trf-nodal-subcurve-boundary]; the pushout supplies semistability at the new point. For a one-vertex tree its image is a singleton and that positive-dimensional fibre disappears. Every surviving tree still has a boundary, by the closed-image and connectedness argument in Step 6. The integer $e$ drops by exactly one, establishing the induction step.

source.place: Appendix B single-component contractions and reduced nodal branch intersections; update of the induction invariants

proof.text: After finitely many steps $e=0$. The remaining map $r_t:R_t\to C$ is proper and every fibre is zero-dimensional; these finite-type fibres have finite point sets. By [lem-trf-proper-finite-fibre-finite-near] it is finite locally on $C$, hence finite. The target $C$ is nodal, the source is reduced and pure one-dimensional by intermediate semistability, $r_t^{-1}(U)\simeq U$ meets every target component, and its geometric fibres are connected by the induction. Therefore [lem-trf-finite-birational-nodal-connected-iso] makes $r_t$ an isomorphism. Its marking map is an isomorphism as well, so it is an isomorphism of pairs. Thus the composite of the constructed elementary pushouts, followed by $r_t$, is exactly $q_\Omega$. Each factor has the asserted properness, complement isomorphism and marking properties. If the initial $e$ is zero this argument supplies the final isomorphism with no pushouts. Neither Corollary 4.4.3(i) nor stable-blowdown uniqueness is used.

title: Geometric fibre maps of semistable modifications are exceptional contraction sequences
statement: Let $K$ be a separably closed field [def-weil-field, def-kun-separably-closed], let $V\subset K$ be a valuation ring with fraction field $K$ (for every $t\ne0$ either $t$ or $t^{-1}$ belongs to $V$), and assume the prime ideals of $V$ form a finite chain. Put $S=\operatorname{Spec}V$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] and $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$. Let $q:(P,M)\to(Q,N)$ be an $\eta$-modification of multipointed $S$-curves [def-trf-multipointed-curve, def-trf-multipointed-curve-modification]. Assume that both pairs are semistable, that $Q_\eta$ is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], and that $N_\eta$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism]. For every $s\in S$ and an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $\kappa(s)$ [def-weil-residue-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], the map $q_\Omega:(P_\Omega,M_\Omega)\to(Q_\Omega,N_\Omega)$ [def-weil-geometric-fibre] is, up to a final isomorphism of pairs, a finite composite of elementary exceptional contractions. Here an elementary exceptional contraction of a semistable pointed $\Omega$-curve $(R,L)$ is the scheme pushout of $R\leftarrow A\to\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, where $A$ is an irreducible component isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1_\Omega$ [def-sc-p1-standard], meets $L\cup R_{\mathrm{sing}}$ in at most two distinct points, and has singleton image under the remaining map to $Q_\Omega$; the quotient is a semistable pointed curve, its marking is the image of $L$ and maps isomorphically from $L$, and the quotient map is proper [def-weil-proper-morphism] and an isomorphism away from $A$. Every intermediate map to $(Q_\Omega,N_\Omega)$ is compatible with the markings. The empty composite is allowed. No connectedness, separatedness or properness of either structural map to $S$ is assumed.
